questions.question: DDT was used at safe concentrations in water, yet falcon eggshells thinned. Explain the mechanism of biomagnification.
questions.solution: DDT is fat-soluble and not excreted, so each organism RETAINS what it absorbs; the next trophic level eats many prey, accumulating all their loads. Water at 0.003 ppb → zooplankton → fish → falcon at ~25 ppm — a 10⁴-fold concentration. Top predators integrate the pollution of the entire chain beneath them, which is why bans must target the whole food web.

questions.question: Fertiliser runoff enriches a lake, yet fish die of OXYGEN shortage. Trace the chain from nutrient to dead fish.
questions.solution: Excess N and P trigger an algal BLOOM → algae die and sink → decomposing bacteria consume oxygen while breaking them down → dissolved O₂ crashes → fish and aerobic life suffocate. The nutrients feed the algae, but the OXYGEN is consumed by the decomposers of the bloom — the crash is a decomposition event, not the bloom itself.

questions.concept: Ozone depletion vs global warming — different problems
questions.question: Students often conflate the ozone hole with global warming. Separate the two: gas class, mechanism, and where each occurs.
questions.solution: Ozone depletion: CFCs release Cl radicals in the STRATOSPHERE that catalytically destroy O₃, raising UV at the surface (skin cancer, cataracts). Global warming: CO₂, CH₄, N₂O absorb outgoing IR in the TROPOSPHERE, trapping heat. Different gases, different altitudes, different mechanisms — one is a UV-screen problem, the other an energy-balance problem.

questions.concept: Acid rain — the two acids and the buffer
questions.question: Why does acid rain kill lakes in granite basins but not in limestone basins?
questions.solution: Acid rain (H₂SO₄ and HNO₃ from SO₂ and NOₓ) is neutralised by carbonate rock: limestone (CaCO₃) buffers the pH, keeping the lake habitable. Granite has no buffering carbonate — the pH drops, aluminium leaches from soil and kills fish gills. Geology, not just acidity, decides the biological damage.

questions.question: Why do deep lakes in summer sometimes suffocate fish at the BOTTOM even though the surface is well oxygenated?
questions.solution: Summer heating stratifies the lake: a warm, oxygen-rich epilimnion floats over a cold, isolated hypolimnion, with the thermocline blocking mixing. The bottom layer's oxygen is consumed by decomposition and not replenished until autumn turnover. Stratification, not total oxygen, controls where life can persist.

questions.question: Clearing hill forests for farmland harms people far downstream. Name three downstream effects and the physical mechanism behind each.
questions.solution: (1) Flooding: tree canopy and roots slow infiltration; rain now runs off fast, so flood peaks are higher and earlier. (2) Siltation: exposed soil erodes, filling reservoirs and raising riverbeds. (3) Reduced dry-season flow: groundwater recharge falls, so springs and base flow shrink. The mechanism is the shift from infiltration to runoff once cover and roots are removed.

questions.concept: Solid waste — the hierarchy of responses
questions.question: Why is burning plastic waste worse than landfilling it, yet recycling beats both? Order the waste-management hierarchy.
questions.solution: Hierarchy: reduce → reuse → recycle → energy recovery → landfill. Burning plastic releases dioxins and furans (persistent toxic organics) plus CO₂ — worse than inert burial. Recycling keeps the material in use, displacing virgin production (the biggest energy saving). Reduction is best because the waste never exists.

questions.question: Why is warming in the Arctic potentially self-accelerating? Identify the feedback loop.
questions.solution: Warming thaws permafrost, releasing stored organic carbon that microbes decompose into CO₂ and CH₄ (a far stronger greenhouse gas per molecule); these warm the atmosphere further, thawing more permafrost — a positive feedback. Positive feedbacks are why climate models include tipping risks beyond linear projections.
